segments.heading: Abstract / Background
segments.text: Advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy complicated by diabetic foot ulceration is a limb-threatening condition associated with progressive foot deformity, recurrent ulceration, infection, impaired wound healing, and a high risk of major amputation. Evidence describing long-term limb preservation following multimodal conservative management remains limited.

segments.heading: Abstract / Case presentation
segments.text: A 43-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and diabetic peripheral neuropathy presented with advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy of the left foot, complicated by a chronic, non-healing dorsal diabetic foot ulcer (3 × 4 cm; Wagner Grade 3; University of Texas Grade 3-D) and a lateral draining sinus. During the earlier course of the disease, magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated extensive Charcot-related bony destruction with findings suggestive of secondary osteomyelitis. The diagnosis was made by the treating podiatric surgeon based on clinical and imaging findings. Microbiological and histopathological confirmation was not available. Despite prior hospitalization, incision and drainage, and approximately 15 days of intravenous antibiotic therapy, satisfactory wound healing was not achieved.

segments.heading: Abstract / Intervention
segments.text: The patient underwent multimodal conservative management comprising continuation of conventional antidiabetic therapy, complete bed rest during the active wound-management period, structured local wound care using Aragvadhadi Kashayam, internal Ayurvedic medications (Pachanamritham Kashayam and Chandraprabha Vati), dietary regulation, and regular clinical follow-up. Custom-made protective footwear had previously been prescribed for the Charcot-related deformity and was used for approximately six months before discontinuation because of discomfort.

segments.heading: Abstract / Outcomes
segments.text: Progressive reduction in wound exudate and slough was followed by healthy granulation tissue formation, complete epithelialization of the dorsal ulcer, and healing of the lateral draining sinus. Limb preservation was achieved without major amputation over approximately four years of follow-up. The patient subsequently regained independent ambulation, resumed routine occupational and daily activities, and maintained functional mobility. The clinical course was documented through serial clinical photographs and follow-up assessments.

segments.heading: Abstract / Conclusion
segments.text: This case describes a favorable long-term outcome, including limb preservation and functional recovery, following multimodal conservative management in a patient with advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy complicated by chronic ulceration. Given the single-case design and the simultaneous use of multiple therapeutic interventions, the independent contribution of individual treatment components cannot be determined. Further prospective studies are warranted.

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: Diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) is one of the most debilitating complications of diabetes mellitus and remains a leading cause of hospitalization, disability, and non-traumatic lower-extremity amputation worldwide. Despite advances in multidisciplinary care, infected and non-healing ulcers continue to impose substantial clinical, psychosocial, and economic burdens on patients and healthcare systems. Recent epidemiological evidence indicates that patients with DFUs remain at considerable risk of major amputation, particularly when ulcers are complicated by infection, neuropathy, or structural deformity (–).

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: Current management of advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy emphasizes prompt diagnosis, meticulous wound care, effective infection control, strict off-loading, optimization of glycemic status, and multidisciplinary follow-up. Conservative management remains the preferred initial approach for many patients, while surgical intervention is reserved for selected cases with severe instability, deformity, or failure of conservative treatment. Nevertheless, prolonged treatment duration, recurrent ulceration, and progression to major amputation continue to be significant challenges, particularly in patients presenting with chronic non-healing wounds (, ).

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: Although numerous studies have described different approaches to diabetic foot management, well-documented reports demonstrating long-term limb preservation with sustained functional recovery in advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy remain limited, particularly following conservative management with prolonged follow-up. We therefore present a patient with advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy complicated by a chronic non-healing diabetic foot ulcer who achieved complete wound healing, long-term limb preservation, restoration of independent ambulation, and sustained functional recovery over four years following an integrative conservative management strategy. This report is presented in accordance with the CARE guidelines.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Patient information
segments.text: A 43-year-old male accountant presented to our Ayurveda hospital with a chronic non-healing ulcer over the dorsal aspect of the left forefoot. His main concerns were persistent wound discharge and failure of satisfactory wound healing despite previous treatment, in the context of established Charcot neuroarthropathy. The ulcer had progressively worsened over the preceding month. He was a known case of type 2 diabetes mellitus and was receiving oral antidiabetic medication (glipizide 5 mg plus metformin 500 mg twice daily). The patient had a documented history of diabetic peripheral neuropathy and Charcot neuroarthropathy involving the left foot. Custom-made protective footwear had previously been prescribed to accommodate and protect the affected foot, with long-term use advised. The patient reported using the footwear for approximately six months but subsequently discontinued its use because of discomfort.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Patient information
segments.text: Before presentation to our institution, the patient had undergone previous treatment for the affected foot, including conservative management for Charcot neuroarthropathy and, during the subsequent complicated foot infection, incision and drainage of a foot abscess followed by approximately 15 days of intravenous piperacillin–tazobactam therapy. Despite these interventions, persistent wound discharge and unsatisfactory healing continued, prompting him to seek further treatment with the objective of limb preservation.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Patient information
segments.text: He reported persistent numbness over the affected foot, consistent with diabetic peripheral neuropathy. His body mass index was 28.4 kg/m². He had a family history of diabetes mellitus but no history of hypertension, chronic kidney disease, previous lower-limb amputation, or other major comorbidities.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Clinical history
segments.text: The patient was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus four years before presentation but was initially non-adherent to antidiabetic medication and lifestyle modifications. In October 2020, he sustained a minor burn injury to the left foot, which subsequently progressed to infection and ulceration. Magnetic resonance imaging performed on 05 October 2020 revealed sclerosis and destruction involving the distal calcaneum, cuboid, and lateral navicular bone, accompanied by marked midfoot edema and sinus formation, with findings suggestive of Charcot neuroarthropathy complicated by secondary osteomyelitis. Computed tomography also demonstrated features consistent with Charcot-related bony destruction. The diagnosis was made by the treating podiatric surgeon based on the available clinical and imaging assessment. Microbiological confirmation through deep-tissue or bone culture and histopathological confirmation through bone biopsy were not available in the records accessible to the authors.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Clinical history
segments.text: Following the diagnosis, conservative management comprising antimicrobial therapy, oral antidiabetic medication, and protective off-loading measures was initiated. Custom-made protective footwear was subsequently prescribed, with long-term use advised. However, the patient reported using the footwear for approximately six months before discontinuing it because of discomfort.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Clinical history
segments.text: In early 2024, following trauma to the toenail of the affected foot, he developed progressive swelling associated with cellulitis, skin breakdown, abscess formation, and a chronic non-healing dorsal foot ulcer. He was admitted to a tertiary-care hospital, where the abscess was managed with incision and drainage, followed by approximately 15 days of intravenous piperacillin–tazobactam, a broad-spectrum antipseudomonal penicillin/β-lactamase inhibitor combination. Additional treatment included oral cefuroxime axetil, trypsin–chymotrypsin, cetirizine, multivitamins, topical wound care, and oxygen therapy.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Clinical history
segments.text: Information regarding wound or deep-tissue bacterial culture results and the specific pathogen(s) targeted during the preceding antimicrobial therapy was not available in the clinical records accessible to the authors. Despite these interventions, wound discharge persisted, and satisfactory healing was not achieved. Given the progressive non-healing ulcer and the recommendation for major amputation, the patient sought treatment at our Ayurveda hospital with the objective of limb preservation.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Clinical findings
segments.text: On admission, the patient was hemodynamically stable and in no acute distress. Clinical examination revealed a 3 × 4 cm ulcer over the dorsal aspect of the left forefoot, extending from the toe tips to the metatarsophalangeal joints of the second, third, and fourth toes (Figure 1A). The ulcer was classified as Wagner Grade 3 and University of Texas Grade 3-D.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Clinical findings
segments.text: More than 80% of the wound bed was covered with thick yellowish-white slough and necrotic tissue, with profuse purulent exudate associated with a foul odor. The wound margins were macerated, and the surrounding skin was erythematous and edematous, consistent with surrounding cellulitis. The dorsum of the foot exhibited xerosis with fissuring, consistent with diabetic autonomic neuropathy. A localized violaceous discoloration of the surrounding skin was also observed, raising concern regarding compromised local tissue perfusion. Diffuse swelling of the affected foot and deformity consistent with established Charcot neuroarthropathy were present.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Clinical findings
segments.text: Peripheral arterial pulsations over the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries were palpable. Overall, the patient presented with a severe infected diabetic foot ulcer characterized by extensive slough and necrotic tissue, profuse foul-smelling purulent discharge, surrounding cellulitis, and underlying Charcot-related foot deformity.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment
segments.text: The diagnostic assessment included detailed clinical evaluation, laboratory investigations, radiological imaging, and Ayurvedic clinical assessment to evaluate the severity of the condition, identify associated complications, and guide subsequent management.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment
segments.text: The diagnosis of advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy was supported by the patient’s history of diabetic peripheral neuropathy, established foot deformity, and radiological evidence of extensive bony destruction and joint disorganization. The presence of a deep diabetic foot ulcer with purulent discharge, surrounding cellulitis, and a lateral draining sinus indicated a severe complicated diabetic foot infection.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment
segments.text: A diagnostic challenge was the interpretation of possible superimposed osteomyelitis in the presence of extensive Charcot-related osseous destruction and bone marrow abnormalities. The MRI performed in 2020 demonstrated extensive Charcot-related bony destruction, marrow oedema, sinus formation, and findings suggestive of secondary osteomyelitis. However, bone biopsy, histopathological examination, and deep-tissue or bone culture results were not available. Therefore, secondary osteomyelitis was considered a suspected complication based on the available clinical and radiological findings and was not microbiologically or histopathologically confirmed.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Hematological investigations
segments.text: Baseline laboratory investigations showed a hemoglobin level of 12.0 g/dL and a total leukocyte count of 7,600/mm³, comprising 51% neutrophils, 45% lymphocytes, 3% eosinophils, 1% monocytes, and no basophils. Inflammatory markers were elevated, with an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 57 mm/hour and a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 12.98 mg/L, indicating an ongoing inflammatory process. The complete laboratory profile, including hematological, glycemic, renal, and biochemical parameters, is presented in Table 1.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Neurological assessment
segments.text: Neurological examination was consistent with diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Assessment of the affected (left) foot using the 10-g Semmes–Weinstein monofilament was not performed because of the extensive dorsal ulcer, active infection, and plantar callosities, which could have interfered with accurate sensory assessment. As monofilament testing could not be reliably performed on the ulcerated foot, sensory assessment was performed on the contralateral foot, together with vibration perception, pin-prick sensation, deep tendon reflexes, and the Neuropathy Disability Score (NDS), to characterize the patient’s underlying diabetic peripheral neuropathy.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Neurological assessment
segments.text: The contralateral (right) foot was evaluated at four standard plantar sites using the 10-g Semmes–Weinstein monofilament. Protective sensation was absent at the distal hallux and diminished over the first, third, and fifth metatarsal heads, indicating loss of protective sensation (LOPS). Vibration perception and pin-prick sensation were impaired. Deep tendon reflex examination demonstrated diminished ankle jerks with preserved knee jerks. The Neuropathy Disability Score (NDS) was 7.5, consistent with moderate diabetic peripheral neuropathy.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Radiological assessment
segments.text: Plain radiographs of the affected (left) foot demonstrated features consistent with chronic Charcot neuroarthropathy, including bony destruction, joint disorganization, and midfoot deformity.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Radiological assessment
segments.text: Magnetic resonance imaging performed on 05 October 2020, during the earlier course of the patient’s disease, demonstrated extensive destruction involving the distal calcaneum, cuboid, and lateral navicular bone, associated with diffuse bone marrow edema. The MRI also demonstrated sinus tract formation from the cuboid region with surrounding soft-tissue edema and findings suggestive of secondary osteomyelitis (Figure 1).

segments.text: These imaging findings formed part of the clinical and radiological assessment on which the treating podiatric surgeon based the diagnosis during the earlier disease course. Microbiological confirmation through deep-tissue or bone culture and histopathological confirmation through bone biopsy were not available in the clinical records accessible to the authors.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Radiological assessment
segments.text: The MRI findings are therefore presented as evidence suggestive of secondary osteomyelitis during the earlier disease course and should not be interpreted as microbiological or histopathological confirmation of osteomyelitis during the 2024 ulcer episode.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Final diagnosis
segments.text: The final diagnosis at presentation to our center was advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy of the left foot complicated by a severe non-healing diabetic foot ulcer (Wagner Grade 3; University of Texas Grade 3-D) in a patient with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and diabetic peripheral neuropathy.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Final diagnosis
segments.text: The patient had a previous clinical and radiological diagnosis of suspected secondary osteomyelitis during the earlier course of Charcot neuroarthropathy. MRI performed in October 2020 demonstrated extensive Charcot-related bony destruction, bone marrow edema, sinus tract formation, and findings suggestive of secondary osteomyelitis. Microbiological and histopathological confirmation of osteomyelitis was not available.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Previous conventional management
segments.text: Before presentation to our institution, the patient had been managed at a tertiary-care hospital for a complicated diabetic foot infection. A localized abscess involving the affected foot was treated with incision and drainage, followed by approximately 15 days of intravenous piperacillin–tazobactam, a broad-spectrum antipseudomonal penicillin/β-lactamase inhibitor combination. Additional treatment included oral cefuroxime axetil, trypsin–chymotrypsin, cetirizine, multivitamins, topical wound care, and oxygen therapy.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Previous conventional management
segments.text: Despite these interventions, the wound continued to exhibit persistent purulent discharge with unsatisfactory healing. Information regarding wound or deep-tissue bacterial culture results and the specific pathogen(s) targeted during the preceding antimicrobial therapy was not available in the clinical records accessible to the authors. Owing to the extensive tissue involvement and poor clinical response, major amputation was advised. Seeking an alternative approach for limb preservation, the patient subsequently presented to our Ayurveda hospital.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Previous conventional management
segments.text: The patient continued his previously prescribed oral antidiabetic medications, comprising glipizide and metformin, throughout the treatment period without modification.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Previous conventional management
segments.text: Before presentation to our institution, custom protective footwear had been prescribed for the Charcot-related foot deformity, with long-term use advised. The patient reported using the footwear for approximately six months before discontinuing it because of discomfort. During the active treatment period at our institution, the patient was maintained on complete bed rest as part of the management strategy for the active wound.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Ayurvedic clinical assessment
segments.text: From an Ayurvedic perspective, the clinical presentation was diagnosed as Madhumehajanya Duṣṭa Vraṇa, a chronic non-healing ulcer associated with Madhumeha (diabetes mellitus). According to Ayurvedic principles, the condition is understood to involve impaired tissue healing associated with pathological interactions between doṣas and duṣyas, contributing to delayed wound repair and chronic ulceration.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Ayurvedic clinical assessment
segments.text: According to the principles described in the Suśruta Saṃhitā, the management of Duṣṭa Vraṇa follows a sequential therapeutic approach consisting of Śodhana (wound cleansing and preparation of the wound bed) followed by Ropaṇa (promotion of wound healing and tissue repair). These principles formed the Ayurvedic therapeutic framework for the management strategy adopted in the present case.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Local wound management
segments.text: Local wound management consisted of twice-daily cleansing, irrigation, and soaking with Aragvadhādi Kaṣāya throughout the active wound-healing period. This regimen was continued until complete epithelialization of the ulcer.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Local wound management
segments.text: Within the Ayurvedic therapeutic framework, the primary objective of Śodhana was wound cleansing and preparation of the wound bed. The local regimen was intended to facilitate the removal of slough and devitalized tissue, reduce excessive wound exudate, maintain wound hygiene, and prepare the wound bed for subsequent healing.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Local wound management
segments.text: Following complete epithelialization, Murivenna, a classical Ayurvedic medicated oil traditionally used in wound care, was applied externally to the healed area to support residual skin recovery and scar maturation.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Internal Ayurvedic management
segments.text: Internal Ayurvedic treatment consisted of Pachanamritham Kaṣāyam and Chandraprabha Vaṭi, administered as part of the treatment regimen. These formulations were selected according to the Ayurvedic diagnosis of Madhumehajanya Duṣṭa Vraṇa.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Internal Ayurvedic management
segments.text: Within the Ayurvedic therapeutic framework, the treatment objectives included addressing the underlying disease process and supporting wound healing and tissue repair. The patient continued his prescribed conventional oral antidiabetic medications without modification throughout the course of Ayurvedic treatment.

segments.heading: Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Internal Ayurvedic management
segments.text: The therapeutic approach was modified according to the stage of wound healing. During the active wound phase, local cleansing, irrigation, and soaking with Aragvadhādi Kaṣāya were continued together with internal Ayurvedic medications and complete bed rest. Following complete epithelialization of the dorsal ulcer and lateral draining sinus, active wound-cleansing procedures were discontinued, and Murivenna was subsequently introduced for external application to support local skin care and scar maturation.

segments.heading: Discussion / Clinical significance of Charcot neuroarthropathy
segments.text: Charcot neuroarthropathy (CN) is one of the most severe complications associated with diabetic peripheral neuropathy and is an important cause of lower-extremity morbidity and limb loss among individuals with diabetes. The coexistence of advanced Charcot deformity and chronic diabetic foot ulceration presents a substantial therapeutic challenge, often requiring prolonged multidisciplinary care and, in severe cases, major amputation. Consequently, successful long-term limb preservation in such patients is of considerable clinical interest (–).

segments.heading: Discussion / Clinical significance of Charcot neuroarthropathy
segments.text: CN is characterized by progressive destruction of bones, joints, and surrounding soft tissues resulting from repetitive mechanical trauma to an insensate foot. Delayed diagnosis and continued mechanical stress during the active phase may contribute to progressive deformity, recurrent ulceration, deep infection, and an increased risk of major amputation. Accordingly, conservative management requires attention to mechanical protection of the affected foot, meticulous wound care, appropriate infection management, optimization of glycaemic status, and long-term surveillance to preserve limb function and prevent further complications (–).

segments.heading: Discussion / Clinical significance of Charcot neuroarthropathy
segments.text: The present case involved advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy complicated by a chronic non-healing diabetic foot ulcer and persistent wound discharge. The patient also had previous MRI findings from 2020 that were suggestive of secondary osteomyelitis. Before presentation to our institution in 2024, he had undergone hospitalization, incision and drainage, and approximately 15 days of intravenous piperacillin–tazobactam therapy without satisfactory wound healing, and major amputation had been advised.

segments.heading: Discussion / Clinical significance of Charcot neuroarthropathy
segments.text: In contrast to reports limited to short-term wound outcomes, this case documents approximately four years of follow-up demonstrating complete healing of both the dorsal ulcer and the lateral draining sinus, restoration of independent ambulation, sustained functional recovery, and long-term limb preservation without recurrence. These outcomes are clinically meaningful because preservation of mobility, maintenance of functional independence, and avoidance of major amputation are important therapeutic goals in patients with advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy. Although causal inferences cannot be drawn from a single case, this report demonstrates that successful long-term limb preservation and functional recovery may be achievable in selected patients receiving comprehensive conservative management.

segments.heading: Discussion / Challenges in conservative limb salvage
segments.text: Limb salvage in advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy extends beyond wound closure and requires simultaneous attention to infection, mechanical protection of the affected foot, prevention of recurrent ulceration, optimization of metabolic status, and restoration of functional mobility. Chronic hyperglycaemia, peripheral neuropathy, repetitive mechanical stress, impaired wound healing, and progressive foot deformity interact to create a complex clinical environment associated with an increased risk of recurrent ulceration, infection, and major amputation. Consequently, successful conservative management requires coordinated multidisciplinary care and long-term surveillance (–).

segments.heading: Discussion / Challenges in conservative limb salvage
segments.text: This case illustrates the complexity of conservative limb salvage in advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy. The patient presented with several adverse clinical features, including advanced deformity, a chronic ulcer, a draining sinus, and a previous MRI examination with findings suggestive of secondary osteomyelitis. However, the available clinical records did not include deep-tissue or bone culture results, and bone biopsy or histopathological confirmation was not available. Therefore, the presence of osteomyelitis should be interpreted as clinically and radiologically suspected rather than definitively confirmed.

segments.heading: Discussion / Challenges in conservative limb salvage
segments.text: Despite these challenges, complete wound healing was achieved without major surgical intervention. The favorable long-term outcome was accompanied by restoration of independent ambulation and absence of ulcer recurrence during approximately four years of follow-up.

segments.heading: Discussion / Challenges in conservative limb salvage
segments.text: Although causal inferences cannot be drawn from a single case, the sustained outcome highlights the importance of comprehensive conservative management, including meticulous wound care, mechanical protection during the active wound-management period, metabolic management, infection management, and regular long-term follow-up in carefully selected patients.

segments.heading: Discussion / Clinical rationale for the management approach
segments.text: Management of advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy complicated by a severe diabetic foot ulcer requires simultaneous attention to local wound conditions, mechanical protection of the affected foot, metabolic control, and prevention of further tissue injury. In the present case, conventional antidiabetic therapy was continued without modification, while complete bed rest was maintained during the active wound-management period to avoid mechanical loading of the affected foot. Local and systemic Ayurvedic interventions were incorporated as components of an integrative conservative management strategy.

segments.heading: Discussion / Clinical rationale for the management approach
segments.text: From an Ayurvedic perspective, the clinical presentation was interpreted as Madhumehajanya Duṣṭa Vraṇa, a chronic non-healing wound associated with Madhumeha (diabetes mellitus). Based on the principles described in the Suśruta Saṃhitā, treatment was planned sequentially, beginning with Śodhana (wound cleansing and preparation of the wound bed), followed by Ropaṇa (promotion of tissue healing and regeneration).

segments.heading: Discussion / Clinical rationale for the management approach
segments.text: Within this therapeutic framework, local wound care with Aragvadhādi Kaṣāya was intended to facilitate wound cleansing and preparation of the wound bed. The internal formulations Pachanamritham Kaṣāyam and Chandraprabha Vaṭi were administered as part of the overall Ayurvedic management strategy. These interventions were provided alongside, rather than in place of, conventional antidiabetic therapy and other supportive measures.

segments.heading: Discussion / Clinical rationale for the management approach
segments.text: Because multiple interventions were implemented concurrently, the contribution of any individual component to the observed outcome cannot be determined.

segments.heading: Discussion / Interpretation of the observed outcomes
segments.text: The clinical course observed in this case provides several clinically relevant observations; however, causal relationships cannot be established from a single case report.

segments.heading: Discussion / Interpretation of the observed outcomes
segments.text: First, wound healing occurred despite suboptimal glycaemic control during the treatment period. Optimization of glycaemic status remains an important component of diabetic foot management. Nevertheless, this observation illustrates the multifactorial nature of wound healing and the potential importance of coordinated management of local wound conditions, mechanical protection, infection, and metabolic factors. The present case should not be interpreted as suggesting that adequate glycaemic control is unnecessary for successful wound healing.

segments.heading: Discussion / Interpretation of the observed outcomes
segments.text: Second, the durability of the outcome is noteworthy. In advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy, recurrent ulceration, progressive deformity, infection, and limb loss remain important long-term concerns. The absence of ulcer recurrence, sinus formation, or clinically documented local infection and the avoidance of major amputation during approximately four years of follow-up suggest sustained clinical stability rather than short-term wound closure alone.

segments.heading: Discussion / Interpretation of the observed outcomes
segments.text: Accordingly, the favorable clinical outcome should be interpreted as an observation following a multimodal integrative conservative management strategy rather than evidence of efficacy of any individual therapeutic component.

segments.heading: Discussion / Interpretation of the observed outcomes
segments.text: Finally, this case emphasizes the importance of evaluating functional recovery in addition to anatomical wound healing. Restoration of independent ambulation, return to routine occupational and daily activities, and successful completion of the Sabarimala pilgrimage indicate meaningful long-term functional recovery from the patient’s perspective. These observations reinforce the value of incorporating functional outcomes alongside wound closure when assessing conservative limb-salvage strategies in advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy.

segments.heading: Discussion / Role of dietary and lifestyle measures within the integrative approach
segments.text: The integrative management strategy also incorporated Ayurvedic dietary and lifestyle recommendations alongside local wound care, internal Ayurvedic formulations, complete bed rest during the active wound-management period, and continuation of conventional diabetes therapy. The independent contribution of these components cannot be determined.

segments.heading: Discussion / Role of dietary and lifestyle measures within the integrative approach
segments.text: From an Ayurvedic perspective, Pathya Āhāra (wholesome dietary regulation) forms an integral component of the management of both Madhumeha and Duṣṭa Vraṇa. The prescribed dietary regimen emphasized foods with a lower glycaemic load while limiting highly processed foods and excessive intake of spicy, salty, and sour foods. These measures were incorporated as supportive components of the overall management strategy.

segments.heading: Discussion / Role of dietary and lifestyle measures within the integrative approach
segments.text: Adequate nocturnal sleep and lifestyle regulation were also advised as supportive measures according to Ayurvedic principles. The specific contribution of these lifestyle interventions to the observed clinical outcome cannot be established in the present case.

The findings should therefore be interpreted as describing the clinical course following a multimodal integrative conservative management strategy rather than demonstrating the efficacy of a specific treatment component (–).

segments.text: The present case has several strengths. First, advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy and wound severity were characterized using clinical assessment, radiological findings, and internationally recognized wound classification systems, including the Wagner and University of Texas classifications.

segments.heading: Discussion / Strengths of this case
segments.text: Second, serial clinical photographs documented the progression from active ulceration to complete wound healing, providing visual documentation of the clinical course.

segments.heading: Discussion / Limitations
segments.text: This report has several limitations. First, as a single-case report, the findings cannot establish treatment efficacy, causality, or generalizability.

segments.heading: Discussion / Limitations
segments.text: Second, although the MRI performed in 2020 demonstrated findings suggestive of secondary osteomyelitis, deep-tissue or bone microbiological culture and histopathological confirmation were unavailable. Therefore, osteomyelitis could not be definitively confirmed, and its subsequent resolution could not be objectively established.

segments.heading: Discussion / Limitations
segments.text: Third, the previous antimicrobial treatment was documented as approximately 15 days of intravenous piperacillin–tazobactam, but information regarding wound culture results and the specific pathogen(s) targeted was not available in the clinical records accessible to the authors.

segments.heading: Discussion / Limitations
segments.text: Fourth, functional recovery was assessed clinically rather than using standardized patient-reported or validated functional outcome measures.

segments.heading: Discussion / Limitations
segments.text: Fifth, follow-up MRI was not performed; therefore, radiological changes in Charcot neuroarthropathy and the status of the previously suspected osteomyelitis could not be evaluated.

segments.heading: Discussion / Limitations
segments.text: Finally, because multiple interventions were implemented concurrently within an integrative conservative management strategy, including conventional diabetes treatment, bed rest, local wound care, internal Ayurvedic formulations, dietary measures, and lifestyle advice, the independent contribution of individual treatment components could not be determined.

segments.heading: Discussion / Limitations
segments.text: Further prospective studies involving larger patient cohorts, standardized functional outcome measures, systematic microbiological assessment when clinically indicated, and serial radiological evaluation are required to evaluate the safety, reproducibility, and clinical outcomes associated with this multimodal management approach.

segments.heading: Discussion / Conclusion
segments.text: This case documents successful long-term limb preservation and functional recovery in a patient with advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy complicated by a severe non-healing diabetic foot ulcer. Complete wound healing, restoration of independent ambulation, and sustained functional recovery without ulcer recurrence or major amputation during approximately four years of follow-up underscore the clinical significance of the observed outcome.

segments.heading: Discussion / Conclusion
segments.text: The favorable clinical course occurred in the context of a multimodal conservative management strategy incorporating conventional diabetes therapy, mechanical protection through complete bed rest during the active wound-management period, local wound care, and Ayurvedic interventions. Because this report describes a single patient receiving multiple concurrent interventions, no conclusions regarding the efficacy or independent contribution of any individual treatment component can be drawn.

segments.heading: Discussion / Conclusion
segments.text: Further prospective studies are warranted to evaluate the safety, reproducibility, and clinical effectiveness of comprehensive conservative management strategies for limb preservation in advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy.

segments.text: The patient expressed satisfaction with the treatment outcome, particularly the complete healing of the ulcer, preservation of the affected limb, and restoration of independent mobility. He reported that he was able to resume his occupational and daily activities and complete the Sabarimala pilgrimage, which he regarded as a major milestone in his recovery.

text:
[b00001] Abstract / Background
Advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy complicated by diabetic foot ulceration is a limb-threatening condition associated with progressive foot deformity, recurrent ulceration, infection, impaired wound healing, and a high risk of major amputation. Evidence describing long-term limb preservation following multimodal conservative management remains limited.

[b00002] Abstract / Case presentation
A 43-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and diabetic peripheral neuropathy presented with advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy of the left foot, complicated by a chronic, non-healing dorsal diabetic foot ulcer (3 × 4 cm; Wagner Grade 3; University of Texas Grade 3-D) and a lateral draining sinus. During the earlier course of the disease, magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated extensive Charcot-related bony destruction with findings suggestive of secondary osteomyelitis. The diagnosis was made by the treating podiatric surgeon based on clinical and imaging findings. Microbiological and histopathological confirmation was not available. Despite prior hospitalization, incision and drainage, and approximately 15 days of intravenous antibiotic therapy, satisfactory wound healing was not achieved.

[b00003] Abstract / Intervention
The patient underwent multimodal conservative management comprising continuation of conventional antidiabetic therapy, complete bed rest during the active wound-management period, structured local wound care using Aragvadhadi Kashayam, internal Ayurvedic medications (Pachanamritham Kashayam and Chandraprabha Vati), dietary regulation, and regular clinical follow-up. Custom-made protective footwear had previously been prescribed for the Charcot-related deformity and was used for approximately six months before discontinuation because of discomfort.

[b00004] Abstract / Outcomes
Progressive reduction in wound exudate and slough was followed by healthy granulation tissue formation, complete epithelialization of the dorsal ulcer, and healing of the lateral draining sinus. Limb preservation was achieved without major amputation over approximately four years of follow-up. The patient subsequently regained independent ambulation, resumed routine occupational and daily activities, and maintained functional mobility. The clinical course was documented through serial clinical photographs and follow-up assessments.

[b00005] Abstract / Conclusion
This case describes a favorable long-term outcome, including limb preservation and functional recovery, following multimodal conservative management in a patient with advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy complicated by chronic ulceration. Given the single-case design and the simultaneous use of multiple therapeutic interventions, the independent contribution of individual treatment components cannot be determined. Further prospective studies are warranted.

[b00006] Introduction
Diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) is one of the most debilitating complications of diabetes mellitus and remains a leading cause of hospitalization, disability, and non-traumatic lower-extremity amputation worldwide. Despite advances in multidisciplinary care, infected and non-healing ulcers continue to impose substantial clinical, psychosocial, and economic burdens on patients and healthcare systems. Recent epidemiological evidence indicates that patients with DFUs remain at considerable risk of major amputation, particularly when ulcers are complicated by infection, neuropathy, or structural deformity (–).

[b00007] Introduction
Among the most devastating complications of diabetic peripheral neuropathy, Charcot neuroarthropathy (CN) is characterized by progressive destruction of bones and joints) represents a particularly challenging condition characterized by progressive destruction of bones and joints secondary to peripheral neuropathy. Delayed diagnosis or inadequate off-loading may result in severe deformity, recurrent ulceration, deep infection, and ultimately limb loss. The coexistence of Charcot deformity with a complicated diabetic foot ulcer substantially increases treatment complexity because successful management requires not only wound healing but also preservation of foot architecture, prevention of recurrent ulceration, and restoration of functional ambulation (–).

[b00008] Introduction
Current management of advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy emphasizes prompt diagnosis, meticulous wound care, effective infection control, strict off-loading, optimization of glycemic status, and multidisciplinary follow-up. Conservative management remains the preferred initial approach for many patients, while surgical intervention is reserved for selected cases with severe instability, deformity, or failure of conservative treatment. Nevertheless, prolonged treatment duration, recurrent ulceration, and progression to major amputation continue to be significant challenges, particularly in patients presenting with chronic non-healing wounds (, ).

[b00009] Introduction
Although numerous studies have described different approaches to diabetic foot management, well-documented reports demonstrating long-term limb preservation with sustained functional recovery in advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy remain limited, particularly following conservative management with prolonged follow-up. We therefore present a patient with advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy complicated by a chronic non-healing diabetic foot ulcer who achieved complete wound healing, long-term limb preservation, restoration of independent ambulation, and sustained functional recovery over four years following an integrative conservative management strategy. This report is presented in accordance with the CARE guidelines.

[b00010] Case presentation / Patient information
A 43-year-old male accountant presented to our Ayurveda hospital with a chronic non-healing ulcer over the dorsal aspect of the left forefoot. His main concerns were persistent wound discharge and failure of satisfactory wound healing despite previous treatment, in the context of established Charcot neuroarthropathy. The ulcer had progressively worsened over the preceding month. He was a known case of type 2 diabetes mellitus and was receiving oral antidiabetic medication (glipizide 5 mg plus metformin 500 mg twice daily). The patient had a documented history of diabetic peripheral neuropathy and Charcot neuroarthropathy involving the left foot. Custom-made protective footwear had previously been prescribed to accommodate and protect the affected foot, with long-term use advised. The patient reported using the footwear for approximately six months but subsequently discontinued its use because of discomfort.

[b00011] Case presentation / Patient information
Before presentation to our institution, the patient had undergone previous treatment for the affected foot, including conservative management for Charcot neuroarthropathy and, during the subsequent complicated foot infection, incision and drainage of a foot abscess followed by approximately 15 days of intravenous piperacillin–tazobactam therapy. Despite these interventions, persistent wound discharge and unsatisfactory healing continued, prompting him to seek further treatment with the objective of limb preservation.

[b00012] Case presentation / Patient information
He reported persistent numbness over the affected foot, consistent with diabetic peripheral neuropathy. His body mass index was 28.4 kg/m². He had a family history of diabetes mellitus but no history of hypertension, chronic kidney disease, previous lower-limb amputation, or other major comorbidities.

[b00013] Case presentation / Clinical history
The patient was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus four years before presentation but was initially non-adherent to antidiabetic medication and lifestyle modifications. In October 2020, he sustained a minor burn injury to the left foot, which subsequently progressed to infection and ulceration. Magnetic resonance imaging performed on 05 October 2020 revealed sclerosis and destruction involving the distal calcaneum, cuboid, and lateral navicular bone, accompanied by marked midfoot edema and sinus formation, with findings suggestive of Charcot neuroarthropathy complicated by secondary osteomyelitis. Computed tomography also demonstrated features consistent with Charcot-related bony destruction. The diagnosis was made by the treating podiatric surgeon based on the available clinical and imaging assessment. Microbiological confirmation through deep-tissue or bone culture and histopathological confirmation through bone biopsy were not available in the records accessible to the authors.

[b00014] Case presentation / Clinical history
Following the diagnosis, conservative management comprising antimicrobial therapy, oral antidiabetic medication, and protective off-loading measures was initiated. Custom-made protective footwear was subsequently prescribed, with long-term use advised. However, the patient reported using the footwear for approximately six months before discontinuing it because of discomfort.

[b00015] Case presentation / Clinical history
In early 2024, following trauma to the toenail of the affected foot, he developed progressive swelling associated with cellulitis, skin breakdown, abscess formation, and a chronic non-healing dorsal foot ulcer. He was admitted to a tertiary-care hospital, where the abscess was managed with incision and drainage, followed by approximately 15 days of intravenous piperacillin–tazobactam, a broad-spectrum antipseudomonal penicillin/β-lactamase inhibitor combination. Additional treatment included oral cefuroxime axetil, trypsin–chymotrypsin, cetirizine, multivitamins, topical wound care, and oxygen therapy.

[b00016] Case presentation / Clinical history
Information regarding wound or deep-tissue bacterial culture results and the specific pathogen(s) targeted during the preceding antimicrobial therapy was not available in the clinical records accessible to the authors. Despite these interventions, wound discharge persisted, and satisfactory healing was not achieved. Given the progressive non-healing ulcer and the recommendation for major amputation, the patient sought treatment at our Ayurveda hospital with the objective of limb preservation.

[b00017] Case presentation / Clinical findings
On admission, the patient was hemodynamically stable and in no acute distress. Clinical examination revealed a 3 × 4 cm ulcer over the dorsal aspect of the left forefoot, extending from the toe tips to the metatarsophalangeal joints of the second, third, and fourth toes (Figure 1A). The ulcer was classified as Wagner Grade 3 and University of Texas Grade 3-D.

[b00018] Case presentation / Clinical findings
More than 80% of the wound bed was covered with thick yellowish-white slough and necrotic tissue, with profuse purulent exudate associated with a foul odor. The wound margins were macerated, and the surrounding skin was erythematous and edematous, consistent with surrounding cellulitis. The dorsum of the foot exhibited xerosis with fissuring, consistent with diabetic autonomic neuropathy. A localized violaceous discoloration of the surrounding skin was also observed, raising concern regarding compromised local tissue perfusion. Diffuse swelling of the affected foot and deformity consistent with established Charcot neuroarthropathy were present.

[b00019] Case presentation / Clinical findings
Peripheral arterial pulsations over the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries were palpable. Overall, the patient presented with a severe infected diabetic foot ulcer characterized by extensive slough and necrotic tissue, profuse foul-smelling purulent discharge, surrounding cellulitis, and underlying Charcot-related foot deformity.

[b00020] Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment
The diagnostic assessment included detailed clinical evaluation, laboratory investigations, radiological imaging, and Ayurvedic clinical assessment to evaluate the severity of the condition, identify associated complications, and guide subsequent management.

[b00021] Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment
The diagnosis of advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy was supported by the patient’s history of diabetic peripheral neuropathy, established foot deformity, and radiological evidence of extensive bony destruction and joint disorganization. The presence of a deep diabetic foot ulcer with purulent discharge, surrounding cellulitis, and a lateral draining sinus indicated a severe complicated diabetic foot infection.

[b00022] Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment
A diagnostic challenge was the interpretation of possible superimposed osteomyelitis in the presence of extensive Charcot-related osseous destruction and bone marrow abnormalities. The MRI performed in 2020 demonstrated extensive Charcot-related bony destruction, marrow oedema, sinus formation, and findings suggestive of secondary osteomyelitis. However, bone biopsy, histopathological examination, and deep-tissue or bone culture results were not available. Therefore, secondary osteomyelitis was considered a suspected complication based on the available clinical and radiological findings and was not microbiologically or histopathologically confirmed.

[b00023] Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Hematological investigations
Baseline laboratory investigations showed a hemoglobin level of 12.0 g/dL and a total leukocyte count of 7,600/mm³, comprising 51% neutrophils, 45% lymphocytes, 3% eosinophils, 1% monocytes, and no basophils. Inflammatory markers were elevated, with an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 57 mm/hour and a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 12.98 mg/L, indicating an ongoing inflammatory process. The complete laboratory profile, including hematological, glycemic, renal, and biochemical parameters, is presented in Table 1.

[b00051] Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Renal function
Baseline renal function was preserved, with blood urea and serum creatinine levels within the normal reference range. Mild hyponatremia (serum sodium, 130 mmol/L) was noted at presentation. Relevant renal and biochemical parameters are summarized in Table 1.

[b00052] Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Liver function
Baseline liver function tests, including serum bilirubin, transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyl transferase, serum proteins, and the albumin–globulin ratio, were within the normal reference ranges (Table 1).

[b00053] Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Urine examination
Routine urine examination was unremarkable, with no evidence of glucosuria, proteinuria, red blood cells, pus cells, or epithelial cells.

[b00054] Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Wound assessment
Detailed wound assessment revealed a 3 × 4 cm ulcer over the dorsal aspect of the left forefoot, extending from the tips of the toes to the metatarsophalangeal joints of the second, third, and fourth toes. The ulcer was classified as Wagner Grade 3 and University of Texas Grade 3-D.

[b00055] Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Wound assessment
More than 80% of the wound bed was covered by thick yellowish-white slough and necrotic tissue, with less than 20% of the wound bed covered by healthy granulation tissue at baseline (Figure 2). Profuse purulent exudate with a foul odor was present, and the wound margins were macerated. The surrounding skin was erythematous and edematous, consistent with cellulitis (Figure 1).

[b00056] Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Wound assessment
A draining sinus was present over the lateral aspect of the foot. The sinus was located in the region corresponding to the sinus tract described on the previous MRI examination. A plantar callosity was also noted at baseline. The affected foot demonstrated diffuse swelling and deformity consistent with chronic Charcot neuroarthropathy. [b00071] Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Neurological assessment
Neurological examination was consistent with diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Assessment of the affected (left) foot using the 10-g Semmes–Weinstein monofilament was not performed because of the extensive dorsal ulcer, active infection, and plantar callosities, which could have interfered with accurate sensory assessment. As monofilament testing could not be reliably performed on the ulcerated foot, sensory assessment was performed on the contralateral foot, together with vibration perception, pin-prick sensation, deep tendon reflexes, and the Neuropathy Disability Score (NDS), to characterize the patient’s underlying diabetic peripheral neuropathy.

[b00072] Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Neurological assessment
The contralateral (right) foot was evaluated at four standard plantar sites using the 10-g Semmes–Weinstein monofilament. Protective sensation was absent at the distal hallux and diminished over the first, third, and fifth metatarsal heads, indicating loss of protective sensation (LOPS). Vibration perception and pin-prick sensation were impaired. Deep tendon reflex examination demonstrated diminished ankle jerks with preserved knee jerks. The Neuropathy Disability Score (NDS) was 7.5, consistent with moderate diabetic peripheral neuropathy.

[b00073] Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Radiological assessment
Plain radiographs of the affected (left) foot demonstrated features consistent with chronic Charcot neuroarthropathy, including bony destruction, joint disorganization, and midfoot deformity.

[b00074] Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Radiological assessment
Magnetic resonance imaging performed on 05 October 2020, during the earlier course of the patient’s disease, demonstrated extensive destruction involving the distal calcaneum, cuboid, and lateral navicular bone, associated with diffuse bone marrow edema. The MRI also demonstrated sinus tract formation from the cuboid region with surrounding soft-tissue edema and findings suggestive of secondary osteomyelitis (Figure 1).

[b00075] Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Radiological assessment
These imaging findings formed part of the clinical and radiological assessment on which the treating podiatric surgeon based the diagnosis during the earlier disease course. Microbiological confirmation through deep-tissue or bone culture and histopathological confirmation through bone biopsy were not available in the clinical records accessible to the authors.

[b00076] Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Radiological assessment
The MRI findings are therefore presented as evidence suggestive of secondary osteomyelitis during the earlier disease course and should not be interpreted as microbiological or histopathological confirmation of osteomyelitis during the 2024 ulcer episode.

[b00077] Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Final diagnosis
The final diagnosis at presentation to our center was advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy of the left foot complicated by a severe non-healing diabetic foot ulcer (Wagner Grade 3; University of Texas Grade 3-D) in a patient with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and diabetic peripheral neuropathy.

[b00078] Case presentation / Diagnostic assessment / Final diagnosis
The patient had a previous clinical and radiological diagnosis of suspected secondary osteomyelitis during the earlier course of Charcot neuroarthropathy. MRI performed in October 2020 demonstrated extensive Charcot-related bony destruction, bone marrow edema, sinus tract formation, and findings suggestive of secondary osteomyelitis. Microbiological and histopathological confirmation of osteomyelitis was not available.

[b00079] Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Previous conventional management
Before presentation to our institution, the patient had been managed at a tertiary-care hospital for a complicated diabetic foot infection. A localized abscess involving the affected foot was treated with incision and drainage, followed by approximately 15 days of intravenous piperacillin–tazobactam, a broad-spectrum antipseudomonal penicillin/β-lactamase inhibitor combination. Additional treatment included oral cefuroxime axetil, trypsin–chymotrypsin, cetirizine, multivitamins, topical wound care, and oxygen therapy.

[b00080] Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Previous conventional management
Despite these interventions, the wound continued to exhibit persistent purulent discharge with unsatisfactory healing. Information regarding wound or deep-tissue bacterial culture results and the specific pathogen(s) targeted during the preceding antimicrobial therapy was not available in the clinical records accessible to the authors. Owing to the extensive tissue involvement and poor clinical response, major amputation was advised. Seeking an alternative approach for limb preservation, the patient subsequently presented to our Ayurveda hospital.

[b00081] Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Previous conventional management
The patient continued his previously prescribed oral antidiabetic medications, comprising glipizide and metformin, throughout the treatment period without modification.

[b00082] Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Previous conventional management
Before presentation to our institution, custom protective footwear had been prescribed for the Charcot-related foot deformity, with long-term use advised. The patient reported using the footwear for approximately six months before discontinuing it because of discomfort. During the active treatment period at our institution, the patient was maintained on complete bed rest as part of the management strategy for the active wound.

[b00083] Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Ayurvedic clinical assessment
From an Ayurvedic perspective, the clinical presentation was diagnosed as Madhumehajanya Duṣṭa Vraṇa, a chronic non-healing ulcer associated with Madhumeha (diabetes mellitus). According to Ayurvedic principles, the condition is understood to involve impaired tissue healing associated with pathological interactions between doṣas and duṣyas, contributing to delayed wound repair and chronic ulceration.

[b00084] Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Ayurvedic clinical assessment
According to the principles described in the Suśruta Saṃhitā, the management of Duṣṭa Vraṇa follows a sequential therapeutic approach consisting of Śodhana (wound cleansing and preparation of the wound bed) followed by Ropaṇa (promotion of wound healing and tissue repair). These principles formed the Ayurvedic therapeutic framework for the management strategy adopted in the present case.

[b00085] Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Local wound management
Local wound management consisted of twice-daily cleansing, irrigation, and soaking with Aragvadhādi Kaṣāya throughout the active wound-healing period. This regimen was continued until complete epithelialization of the ulcer.

[b00086] Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Local wound management
Within the Ayurvedic therapeutic framework, the primary objective of Śodhana was wound cleansing and preparation of the wound bed. The local regimen was intended to facilitate the removal of slough and devitalized tissue, reduce excessive wound exudate, maintain wound hygiene, and prepare the wound bed for subsequent healing.

[b00087] Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Local wound management
Following complete epithelialization, Murivenna, a classical Ayurvedic medicated oil traditionally used in wound care, was applied externally to the healed area to support residual skin recovery and scar maturation.

[b00088] Case presentation / Therapeutic intervention / Internal Ayurvedic management

[b00118] Discussion / Clinical significance of Charcot neuroarthropathy
Charcot neuroarthropathy (CN) is one of the most severe complications associated with diabetic peripheral neuropathy and is an important cause of lower-extremity morbidity and limb loss among individuals with diabetes. The coexistence of advanced Charcot deformity and chronic diabetic foot ulceration presents a substantial therapeutic challenge, often requiring prolonged multidisciplinary care and, in severe cases, major amputation. Consequently, successful long-term limb preservation in such patients is of considerable clinical interest (–).

[b00119] Discussion / Clinical significance of Charcot neuroarthropathy
CN is characterized by progressive destruction of bones, joints, and surrounding soft tissues resulting from repetitive mechanical trauma to an insensate foot. Delayed diagnosis and continued mechanical stress during the active phase may contribute to progressive deformity, recurrent ulceration, deep infection, and an increased risk of major amputation. Accordingly, conservative management requires attention to mechanical protection of the affected foot, meticulous wound care, appropriate infection management, optimization of glycaemic status, and long-term surveillance to preserve limb function and prevent further complications (–).

[b00120] Discussion / Clinical significance of Charcot neuroarthropathy
The present case involved advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy complicated by a chronic non-healing diabetic foot ulcer and persistent wound discharge. The patient also had previous MRI findings from 2020 that were suggestive of secondary osteomyelitis. Before presentation to our institution in 2024, he had undergone hospitalization, incision and drainage, and approximately 15 days of intravenous piperacillin–tazobactam therapy without satisfactory wound healing, and major amputation had been advised.

[b00121] Discussion / Clinical significance of Charcot neuroarthropathy
In contrast to reports limited to short-term wound outcomes, this case documents approximately four years of follow-up demonstrating complete healing of both the dorsal ulcer and the lateral draining sinus, restoration of independent ambulation, sustained functional recovery, and long-term limb preservation without recurrence. These outcomes are clinically meaningful because preservation of mobility, maintenance of functional independence, and avoidance of major amputation are important therapeutic goals in patients with advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy. Although causal inferences cannot be drawn from a single case, this report demonstrates that successful long-term limb preservation and functional recovery may be achievable in selected patients receiving comprehensive conservative management.

[b00122] Discussion / Challenges in conservative limb salvage
Limb salvage in advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy extends beyond wound closure and requires simultaneous attention to infection, mechanical protection of the affected foot, prevention of recurrent ulceration, optimization of metabolic status, and restoration of functional mobility. Chronic hyperglycaemia, peripheral neuropathy, repetitive mechanical stress, impaired wound healing, and progressive foot deformity interact to create a complex clinical environment associated with an increased risk of recurrent ulceration, infection, and major amputation. Consequently, successful conservative management requires coordinated multidisciplinary care and long-term surveillance (–).

[b00123] Discussion / Challenges in conservative limb salvage
This case illustrates the complexity of conservative limb salvage in advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy. The patient presented with several adverse clinical features, including advanced deformity, a chronic ulcer, a draining sinus, and a previous MRI examination with findings suggestive of secondary osteomyelitis. However, the available clinical records did not include deep-tissue or bone culture results, and bone biopsy or histopathological confirmation was not available. Therefore, the presence of osteomyelitis should be interpreted as clinically and radiologically suspected rather than definitively confirmed.

[b00124] Discussion / Challenges in conservative limb salvage
Despite these challenges, complete wound healing was achieved without major surgical intervention. The favorable long-term outcome was accompanied by restoration of independent ambulation and absence of ulcer recurrence during approximately four years of follow-up.

[b00125] Discussion / Challenges in conservative limb salvage
Although causal inferences cannot be drawn from a single case, the sustained outcome highlights the importance of comprehensive conservative management, including meticulous wound care, mechanical protection during the active wound-management period, metabolic management, infection management, and regular long-term follow-up in carefully selected patients.

[b00126] Discussion / Clinical rationale for the management approach
Management of advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy complicated by a severe diabetic foot ulcer requires simultaneous attention to local wound conditions, mechanical protection of the affected foot, metabolic control, and prevention of further tissue injury. In the present case, conventional antidiabetic therapy was continued without modification, while complete bed rest was maintained during the active wound-management period to avoid mechanical loading of the affected foot. Local and systemic Ayurvedic interventions were incorporated as components of an integrative conservative management strategy.

[b00127] Discussion / Clinical rationale for the management approach
From an Ayurvedic perspective, the clinical presentation was interpreted as Madhumehajanya Duṣṭa Vraṇa, a chronic non-healing wound associated with Madhumeha (diabetes mellitus). Based on the principles described in the Suśruta Saṃhitā, treatment was planned sequentially, beginning with Śodhana (wound cleansing and preparation of the wound bed), followed by Ropaṇa (promotion of tissue healing and regeneration).

[b00128] Discussion / Clinical rationale for the management approach
Within this therapeutic framework, local wound care with Aragvadhādi Kaṣāya was intended to facilitate wound cleansing and preparation of the wound bed. The internal formulations Pachanamritham Kaṣāyam and Chandraprabha Vaṭi were administered as part of the overall Ayurvedic management strategy. These interventions were provided alongside, rather than in place of, conventional antidiabetic therapy and other supportive measures.

[b00129] Discussion / Clinical rationale for the management approach
Because multiple interventions were implemented concurrently, the contribution of any individual component to the observed outcome cannot be determined.

[b00130] Discussion / Interpretation of the observed outcomes
The clinical course observed in this case provides several clinically relevant observations; however, causal relationships cannot be established from a single case report.

[b00131] Discussion / Interpretation of the observed outcomes
First, wound healing occurred despite suboptimal glycaemic control during the treatment period. Optimization of glycaemic status remains an important component of diabetic foot management. Nevertheless, this observation illustrates the multifactorial nature of wound healing and the potential importance of coordinated management of local wound conditions, mechanical protection, infection, and metabolic factors. The present case should not be interpreted as suggesting that adequate glycaemic control is unnecessary for successful wound healing.

[b00132] Discussion / Interpretation of the observed outcomes
Second, the durability of the outcome is noteworthy. In advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy, recurrent ulceration, progressive deformity, infection, and limb loss remain important long-term concerns. The absence of ulcer recurrence, sinus formation, or clinically documented local infection and the avoidance of major amputation during approximately four years of follow-up suggest sustained clinical stability rather than short-term wound closure alone.

[b00133] Discussion / Interpretation of the observed outcomes
Accordingly, the favorable clinical outcome should be interpreted as an observation following a multimodal integrative conservative management strategy rather than evidence of efficacy of any individual therapeutic component.

[b00134] Discussion / Interpretation of the observed outcomes
Finally, this case emphasizes the importance of evaluating functional recovery in addition to anatomical wound healing. Restoration of independent ambulation, return to routine occupational and daily activities, and successful completion of the Sabarimala pilgrimage indicate meaningful long-term functional recovery from the patient’s perspective. These observations reinforce the value of incorporating functional outcomes alongside wound closure when assessing conservative limb-salvage strategies in advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy.

[b00135] Discussion / Role of dietary and lifestyle measures within the integrative approach
The integrative management strategy also incorporated Ayurvedic dietary and lifestyle recommendations alongside local wound care, internal Ayurvedic formulations, complete bed rest during the active wound-management period, and continuation of conventional diabetes therapy. The independent contribution of these components cannot be determined.

[b00136] Discussion / Role of dietary and lifestyle measures within the integrative approach
From an Ayurvedic perspective, Pathya Āhāra (wholesome dietary regulation) forms an integral component of the management of both Madhumeha and Duṣṭa Vraṇa. The prescribed dietary regimen emphasized foods with a lower glycaemic load while limiting highly processed foods and excessive intake of spicy, salty, and sour foods. These measures were incorporated as supportive components of the overall management strategy.

[b00137] Discussion / Role of dietary and lifestyle measures within the integrative approach
Adequate nocturnal sleep and lifestyle regulation were also advised as supportive measures according to Ayurvedic principles. The specific contribution of these lifestyle interventions to the observed clinical outcome cannot be established in the present case.

[b00138] Discussion / Role of dietary and lifestyle measures within the integrative approach
Because the patient received multiple concurrent interventions, including conventional diabetes therapy, previous antimicrobial and surgical management, bed rest, local wound care, internal Ayurvedic formulations, dietary regulation, and lifestyle measures, the observed outcome cannot be attributed to any individual intervention. The findings should therefore be interpreted as describing the clinical course following a multimodal integrative conservative management strategy rather than demonstrating the efficacy of a specific treatment component (–).

[b00139] Discussion / Strengths of this case
The present case has several strengths. First, advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy and wound severity were characterized using clinical assessment, radiological findings, and internationally recognized wound classification systems, including the Wagner and University of Texas classifications.

[b00140] Discussion / Strengths of this case
Second, serial clinical photographs documented the progression from active ulceration to complete wound healing, providing visual documentation of the clinical course.

[b00141] Discussion / Strengths of this case
Third, the approximately four-year follow-up demonstrated sustained limb preservation, independent ambulation, and absence of ulcer recurrence or major amputation, extending beyond short-term wound-healing outcomes commonly reported in individual cases.

[b00142] Discussion / Strengths of this case
Finally, the management strategy and therapeutic interventions have been described in detail, including the concurrent use of conventional antidiabetic therapy and Ayurvedic interventions, thereby improving transparency regarding the multimodal nature of the management approach ().

[b00143] Discussion / Limitations
This report has several limitations. First, as a single-case report, the findings cannot establish treatment efficacy, causality, or generalizability.

[b00144] Discussion / Limitations
Second, although the MRI performed in 2020 demonstrated findings suggestive of secondary osteomyelitis, deep-tissue or bone microbiological culture and histopathological confirmation were unavailable. Therefore, osteomyelitis could not be definitively confirmed, and its subsequent resolution could not be objectively established.

[b00145] Discussion / Limitations
Third, the previous antimicrobial treatment was documented as approximately 15 days of intravenous piperacillin–tazobactam, but information regarding wound culture results and the specific pathogen(s) targeted was not available in the clinical records accessible to the authors.

[b00146] Discussion / Limitations
Fourth, functional recovery was assessed clinically rather than using standardized patient-reported or validated functional outcome measures.

[b00147] Discussion / Limitations
Fifth, follow-up MRI was not performed; therefore, radiological changes in Charcot neuroarthropathy and the status of the previously suspected osteomyelitis could not be evaluated.

[b00148] Discussion / Limitations
Finally, because multiple interventions were implemented concurrently within an integrative conservative management strategy, including conventional diabetes treatment, bed rest, local wound care, internal Ayurvedic formulations, dietary measures, and lifestyle advice, the independent contribution of individual treatment components could not be determined.

[b00149] Discussion / Limitations
Further prospective studies involving larger patient cohorts, standardized functional outcome measures, systematic microbiological assessment when clinically indicated, and serial radiological evaluation are required to evaluate the safety, reproducibility, and clinical outcomes associated with this multimodal management approach.

[b00150] Discussion / Conclusion
This case documents successful long-term limb preservation and functional recovery in a patient with advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy complicated by a severe non-healing diabetic foot ulcer. Complete wound healing, restoration of independent ambulation, and sustained functional recovery without ulcer recurrence or major amputation during approximately four years of follow-up underscore the clinical significance of the observed outcome.

[b00151] Discussion / Conclusion
The favorable clinical course occurred in the context of a multimodal conservative management strategy incorporating conventional diabetes therapy, mechanical protection through complete bed rest during the active wound-management period, local wound care, and Ayurvedic interventions. Because this report describes a single patient receiving multiple concurrent interventions, no conclusions regarding the efficacy or independent contribution of any individual treatment component can be drawn.

[b00152] Discussion / Conclusion
Further prospective studies are warranted to evaluate the safety, reproducibility, and clinical effectiveness of comprehensive conservative management strategies for limb preservation in advanced Charcot neuroarthropathy.
